description: In each jhāna the body is pervaded: by rapture and bliss born of seclusion like bath-powder kneaded with water; by rapture and bliss born of concentration like a lake fed from a spring; by bliss without rapture like submerged lotuses; by pure bright mind like a man wrapped in white cloth.
Perception of light and vision of forms arising in concentration, which vanish when doubt, inattention, fear, elation and the other imperfections arise, and stabilise when these are abandoned.
With the concentrated mind directed to knowledge and vision, one sees the body as material and consciousness bound up with it, like a thread strung through a clear beryl gem.
A mind-made body drawn out of this body, complete in all its limbs, like a reed from its sheath, a sword from its scabbard, a snake from its slough.

Becoming many and one, appearing and vanishing, passing through walls, diving into earth, walking on water, flying cross-legged, touching sun and moon, wielding mastery up to the Brahmā world; the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, past lives, the divine eye.

In the three watches of the night of awakening: recollection of past lives, the divine eye seeing beings pass away and reappear, and the knowledge of the destruction of the effluents — 'ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose'.
The bodhisatta's recollection of entering the first jhāna as a child in the shade of a jambu tree, recognised as 'the path to awakening', and his realisation that he need not fear that pleasure.
During his austerities the bodhisatta felt violent winds, pains and burning in the body and became emaciated, yet the painful feelings did not overpower his mind; these did not lead to awakening.
The dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arising in the hearer: 'whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation' — the sign of stream-entry (Koṇḍañña, Sāriputta).
When the wheel of Dhamma was set rolling, the cry of the gods rose to the Brahmā world, the ten-thousandfold world-system shook, and an immeasurable light appeared.

Emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling the mental formation arises first, then bodily, then verbal; three contacts touch him — empty, signless, undirected — and the mind inclines to seclusion.
At the peak of perception the monk thinks that intending and willing would be worse for him, so neither intends nor wills; those perceptions cease and others do not arise: he touches cessation.
The nun Paṭācārā, drawing down the wick of her lamp, was liberated as the flame went out.
At Vakkali's death the Buddha shows the monks a cloud of smoke moving in all directions: Māra searching for Vakkali's consciousness, which was unestablished.
On hearing the brief teaching 'in the seen only the seen' Bāhiya's mind was freed at once from the effluents.
The uninstructed person struck by painful feeling adds grief like a second dart; the noble disciple feels the bodily pain alone.
When mindfulness of breathing has been developed, even one's last breaths are known as they cease, not unknown.
